summary.text: Assuming the first asserted identity holds indefinitely, shifting by one forces a Fibonacci recurrence; using the computed values at indices 3773 and 3774, a modular Fibonacci calculation modulo \(195318521017\) shows that this number divides both \(a(249580077006)\) and \(a(249580077007)\). Thus their gcd \(g\ge2\); writing their sum as \(gq\) with \(q\ge2\), the defining recurrence and the asserted identity at the next index would require \(g+q=1+gq\), impossible because \(1+gq-g-q=(g-1)(q-1)>0\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(a_1=a_2=1\), and for \(n\ge 3\) define
\[
a_n=g_n+\frac{a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}}{g_n},
\qquad g_n=\gcd(a_{n-1},a_{n-2}).
\]
We will prove that the conjecture is false. In fact, it is enough to disprove its first asserted identity
\[
a_n=1+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}\qquad(n\ge 3775),                 \tag{1}
\]
because the full conjecture asserts this identity together with two others.

We argue by contradiction. Assume that (1) holds for every \(n\ge 3775\).

First note that every term \(a_n\), for \(n\ge 1\), is positive. This follows by induction. It is true for \(a_1=a_2=1\). If two consecutive terms are positive, then their gcd is positive, and hence the next term, which is that gcd plus a nonnegative integer, is positive as well.

We next record the finite computation of the two terms at indices 3773 and 3774. A convenient way to perform it is to iterate the map
\[
T(u,v)=\left(v,\gcd(u,v)+\frac{u+v}{\gcd(u,v)}\right).
\]
Starting from \((1,1)=(a_1,a_2)\), a direct induction on \(r\) gives
\[
T^r(1,1)=(a_{r+1},a_{r+2}).
\]
Thus 3772 applications of \(T\), using the Euclidean algorithm for each gcd and exact integer division by that gcd, give
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{3773}={}&,\\[2mm]
a_{3774}={}&.
\end{aligned}                                                    \tag{2}
\]
Only the residues of these numbers modulo a certain integer will ultimately be needed, but the displayed exact values make the finite computation unambiguous.

Now put
\[
b_n=a_n+1.
\]
Under assumption (1), for every \(n\ge 3775\) we have
\[
b_n=a_n+1
     =2+a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}
     =b_{n-1}+b_{n-2}.                                  \tag{3}
\]
Let \(F_0=0\), \(F_1=1\), and \(F_{r+2}=F_{r+1}+F_r\) be the Fibonacci numbers. Equation (3) implies that for every integer \(j\ge 0\),
\[
b_{3774+j}=b_{3774}F_{j+1}+b_{3773}F_j.                 \tag{4}
\]
For completeness, this is proved as follows. When \(j=0\), the right side is
\(b_{3774}F_1+b_{3773}F_0=b_{3774}\). When \(j=1\), it is
\(b_{3774}F_2+b_{3773}F_1=b_{3774}+b_{3773}=b_{3775}\),
where the last equality is (3). For \(j\ge 2\), if the formula is known for the preceding two values, then (3) and the Fibonacci recurrence give
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{3774+j}
 &=b_{3773+j}+b_{3772+j}\\
 &=b_{3774}(F_j+F_{j-1})+b_{3773}(F_{j-1}+F_{j-2})\\
 &=b_{3774}F_{j+1}+b_{3773}F_j.
\end{aligned}
\]
This establishes (4).

We now choose
\[
p=195318521017
\]
and work modulo \(p\). Reducing the two exact values in (2) gives
\[
a_{3774}\equiv 99768150821\pmod p,
\qquad
a_{3773}\equiv 77940394258\pmod p.                    \tag{5}
\]
No primality property of \(p\) is needed; it is simply a common divisor that will be forced upon two consecutive terms.

Set
\[
j=249580073233.
\]
A finite Fibonacci computation modulo \(p\) gives
\[
F_j\equiv21827756563\pmod p,
\qquad
F_{j+1}\equiv139205883321\pmod p.                       \tag{6}
\]
It also gives
\[
F_{j-1}\equiv117378126758\pmod p.                       \tag{7}
\]
Here is an explicit reproducible method for this modular computation. Starting with \((F_0,F_1)=(0,1)\), read the binary expansion
\[
j=(11101000011100001000011011000100010001)_2.
\]
For each current pair \((F_k,F_{k+1})=(u,v)\), use the fast-doubling identities
\[
F_{2k}=u(2v-u),
\qquad
F_{2k+1}=u^2+v^2,
\]
and, according as the next binary digit is 0 or 1, replace the pair by
\[
(F_{2k},F_{2k+1})
\quad\hbox{or}\quad
(F_{2k+1},F_{2k}+F_{2k+1}),
\]
reducing after every operation modulo \(p\). This yields the pair in (6). Then the Fibonacci recurrence gives
\[
F_{j-1}\equiv F_{j+1}-F_j
 \equiv139205883321-21827756563
 =117378126758\pmod p,
\]
which is (7).

Apply formula (4) first at this value of \(j\). Since
\[
3774+j=249580077007,
\]
we obtain, using (5) and (6),
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{249580077007}+1
&=b_{249580077007}\\
&\equiv(99768150821+1)\,139205883321
 +(77940394258+1)\,21827756563\pmod p.
\end{aligned}
\]
The integer on the right before reduction is
\[
15589577514788957011679
 =195318521017\cdot79816176334+1.
\]
Consequently
\[
a_{249580077007}+1\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
and hence
\[
p\mid a_{249580077007}.                                \tag{8}
\]

Apply (4) once more, now with \(j-1=249580073232\). Since
\[
3774+(j-1)=249580077006,
\]
and since the relevant consecutive Fibonacci residues are, by (7) and (6),
\[
F_{j-1}\equiv117378126758,
\qquad F_j\equiv21827756563\pmod p,
\]
we get
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{249580077006}+1
&\equiv(99768150821+1)\,21827756563
 +(77940394258+1)\,117378126758\pmod p.
\end{aligned}
\]
This time the unreduced integer is
\[
11326212385784681827108
 =195318521017\cdot57988419771+1.
\]
Therefore
\[
a_{249580077006}+1\equiv1\pmod p,
\]
so
\[
p\mid a_{249580077006}.                                \tag{9}
\]

We now obtain the contradiction at the next index. Define
\[
N=249580077008,
\qquad x=a_{N-1}=a_{249580077007},
\qquad y=a_{N-2}=a_{249580077006},
\]
and let
\[
g=\gcd(x,y),
\qquad q=\frac{x+y}{g}.
\]
By (8) and (9), \(p\) divides both \(x\) and \(y\), so it divides their gcd \(g\). Since \(x,y>0\), their gcd is positive. Hence
\[
g\ge p=195318521017\ge2.                               \tag{10}
\]

Also, because \(g\) divides both \(x\) and \(y\), write
\[
x=gr,
\qquad y=gs
\]
for nonnegative integers \(r,s\). Positivity of \(x,y,g\) implies \(r,s\ge1\). Therefore
\[
q=\frac{x+y}{g}=r+s\ge2,                                \tag{11}
\]
and
\[
x+y=gq.                                                  \tag{12}
\]

The defining recurrence for the actual sequence at index \(N\) says
\[
a_N=g+q.                                                  \tag{13}
\]
On the other hand, \(N\ge3775\), so the assumed identity (1) says
\[
a_N=1+x+y=1+gq.                                          \tag{14}
\]
Combining (13) and (14) gives
\[
g+q=1+gq.                                                 \tag{15}
\]
But (10) and (11) imply \(g,q\ge2\). Thus
\[
(g-1)(q-1)\ge1.
\]
Expanding this inequality gives
\[
gq-g-q+1\ge1,
\]
or equivalently
\[
gq\ge g+q.                                               \tag{16}
\]
Equation (15), however, says \(g+q=1+gq>gq\), directly contradicting (16).

Thus identity (1) cannot hold for every \(n\ge3775\). Since the stated OEIS conjecture includes (1) as its first required equality, the conjunction of all three claimed formulas is false.
